rubric.why: Identifies the organism and the absence of oxygen in alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.description: Alcoholic fermentation is carried out by yeast in the absence of oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying yeast and anaerobic conditions.

rubric.why: Identifies the products of alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.description: Glucose is converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide, releasing energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both products.

modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose by yeast.
Glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy (C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂ + energy).

items.followUp: Explain how pH affects the rate of enzyme action.

rubric.why: Defines an enzyme by its role as a catalyst in living organisms.
rubric.description: An enzyme is a biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining an enzyme as a biological catalyst.

rubric.why: Explains why enzyme action initially increases with temperature.
rubric.description: As temperature rises, enzyme and substrate molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more frequently, increasing the reaction rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased kinetic energy to more frequent collisions.

rubric.why: Identifies the temperature at which enzyme activity reaches its maximum.
rubric.description: The rate reaches its maximum at the enzyme’s optimum temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the optimum temperature or maximum activity.

rubric.why: Explains the decrease in enzyme activity above the optimum temperature.
rubric.description: Above the optimum, the enzyme may denature, changing its active site and decreasing the reaction rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting denaturation or a changed active site with a decrease in rate.

modelAnswer: An enzyme is a biological catalyst that speeds up chemical reactions in living organisms.
As temperature rises, enzyme and substrate molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more frequently, so the reaction rate increases.
The rate reaches its maximum at the enzyme’s optimum temperature.
Above the optimum, the enzyme may denature and its active site changes shape, causing the rate to decrease.
